idiom_name: Pundit policy objects (authorize record, :action? + policy_scope) or CanCanCan Ability with authorize!/can?
implementation_notes: Ruby's convention is a policy object per resource rather than a global matrix. With Pundit each resource has a policy class whose query methods (update?, destroy?) are the decision points: controllers call authorize @record, :update?, collections go through policy_scope, and roles are read from current_user (current_user.pauser? or a roles association). Because a forgotten authorize is the classic hole, Pundit offers verify_authorized/verify_policy_scoped after_actions that raise when an action neither authorized nor scoped. CanCanCan expresses the same in one Ability class - can :manage, Post if user.admin?, can :pause, Transfers if user.pauser? - checked with authorize! (raises CanCan::AccessDenied mapped to 403) or can? in views, and its rules carry conditions (can :update, Post, user_id: user.id) so ownership needs no separate mechanism. Both are the decision layer; the enforcement seam is the controller before_action plus the exception handler that maps denial to 403, and roles come from the logged-in current_user, not from parameters.
code_sketch:
class PostPolicy < ApplicationPolicy
  def update? = user.pauser? || record.author_id == user.id
  def destroy? = user.admin?
end

class PostsController < ApplicationController
  def update
    @post = Post.find(params[:id])
    authorize @post, :update?          # raises Pundit::NotAuthorizedError -> 403
    @post.update!(post_params)
  end
end
pitfalls: A controller action that forgets authorize is silently open; enable after_action :verify_authorized so the omission raises in tests.
Index actions bypass authorize by design; a missing policy_scope leaks other tenants' rows, so scope collections explicitly.
Deriving the actor from a parameter or an unverified session flag makes the policy forgeable; use current_user only.
CanCanCan's :manage alias expands to every action and hides missing granular rules; enumerate actions for security-sensitive resources.
A policy that loads user.roles inside every method turns each page into N+1 queries; preload the roles on current_user.
